title: Arjuna's Despair
summary: On the battlefield of Kurukshetra, Arjuna sees teachers, elders and kinsmen on both sides and collapses in grief. He puts down his bow and refuses to fight. The chapter is the honest picture of a person frozen by fear, attachment and confusion about what is right.

title: The Yoga of Knowledge
summary: Krishna begins by shaking Arjuna out of weakness, then teaches that the self is eternal and the body temporary, that pleasure and pain come and go like seasons, and that one has a right to one's work but not to its fruits. The chapter ends with the portrait of a person of steady wisdom whose desires enter them like rivers into a full ocean.

title: The Yoga of Action
summary: Nobody can avoid acting, so the question is how to act. Krishna teaches work done as an offering, without attachment, and explains that leaders set the pattern others follow. He names lust and anger, born of passion, as the enemies that cover wisdom like smoke covers fire.

title: Knowledge, Action and Renunciation
summary: Krishna explains why he appears whenever dharma declines, how to see action in inaction, and how knowledge burns the bonds of karma. He urges Arjuna to approach a teacher with humility, warns that a doubting person finds happiness nowhere, and tells him to cut doubt with the sword of knowledge and stand up.

title: Renunciation and Action
summary: Renouncing action and acting without attachment both lead to freedom, but acting is easier. The person who works without selfish motive is untouched by results, like a lotus leaf by water. Sense pleasures have a beginning and an end and so breed misery; lasting peace comes from knowing the Divine as the friend of all beings.

title: The Yoga of Meditation
summary: One must lift oneself by one's own mind, which is both friend and enemy. Krishna describes meditation, moderation in eating, sleep and work, and the patient practice of bringing the wandering mind back again and again. When Arjuna protests that the mind is harder to control than the wind, Krishna answers with practice and detachment, and promises that no sincere effort is ever lost.

title: Knowledge of the Absolute
summary: Krishna describes himself as the taste in water, the light of the sun, the strength of the strong free from desire. Four kinds of people turn to him: the distressed, the seeker of wealth, the curious and the wise. Desire and aversion delude everyone born, and the divine illusion is hard to cross except by surrender.

title: Attaining the Supreme
summary: Whatever one remembers at the end of life shapes what one becomes, so Krishna asks Arjuna to remember him always and do his duty. The chapter describes the cycles of cosmic time and the path by which the devoted mind reaches what is beyond return.

title: The Most Confidential Knowledge
summary: Devotion is the king of knowledge, joyful to practice. Krishna accepts a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water offered with love, asks that every act be made an offering, promises to carry what his devotees lack, and declares that even a person of very bad conduct who turns to him sincerely is quickly set right.

title: The Divine Glories
summary: Intelligence, knowledge, forgiveness, truthfulness, calm, fear and fearlessness all arise from the Divine. Krishna lists his manifestations among all things, and says that whatever is powerful, beautiful or glorious springs from a spark of his splendour.

title: The Universal Form
summary: Arjuna is given divine sight and sees the universal form, with all beings entering its mouths like rivers into the sea. Krishna declares himself Time, the destroyer of worlds, and tells Arjuna that the outcome is already set and he need only be an instrument. Overwhelmed, Arjuna asks for the familiar form back.

title: The Yoga of Devotion
summary: Krishna lays out a ladder of practice: fix the mind on him; if not, practise; if not, work for him; if not, at least renounce the fruits of action, which brings peace. He then describes the devotee he loves: free of envy, friendly to all, equal in pleasure and pain, not disturbing others and not disturbed by them.

title: The Field and Its Knower
summary: The body is the field and the self is the knower of the field. Real knowledge is a way of living: humility, non-violence, tolerance, simplicity, self-control, detachment from the entanglements of home and family, and steadiness amid wanted and unwanted events. The self is not the doer and is untouched, like the sky.

title: The Three Qualities of Nature
summary: All of nature works through three qualities: goodness, which binds through attachment to happiness and knowledge; passion, which binds through endless desire and activity; and inertia, which binds through laziness, sleep and delusion. Krishna describes how each shows itself and how the person who rises above them behaves.

title: The Supreme Person
summary: The world is pictured as an upside-down banyan tree whose roots are above and whose branches grow downward, nourished by the qualities of nature. Its deep roots of attachment must be cut with the axe of detachment. Krishna sits in every heart, and from him come memory, knowledge and forgetting.

title: Divine and Demonic Natures
summary: Fearlessness, purity, charity, self-control, truthfulness, freedom from anger, compassion, gentleness, steadiness and forgiveness mark the divine nature. Pride, arrogance, conceit, anger and harshness mark the demonic. Lust, anger and greed are called the three gates to hell, and the chapter closes by urging action guided by wisdom rather than whim.

title: The Three Kinds of Faith
summary: A person is made of their faith. Food, worship, discipline and charity each take three forms according to the qualities of nature. Discipline of speech is speaking what is true, pleasant and beneficial; discipline of mind is calm, gentleness, silence and self-control.

title: Liberation Through Renunciation
summary: Krishna draws the whole teaching together: do not abandon duty out of fear or discomfort, give up only the attachment to results; see that every action has five causes and you are never the sole doer; know that happiness which tastes like poison first and nectar later is the real kind. He tells Arjuna to deliberate fully and then act as he chooses, promises to free him from all fear, and Arjuna answers that his doubt is gone and he will act.
